sections.overview: The Swan Goose is a long-necked migratory goose of eastern Asia, breeding mainly in Mongolia, northeastern China, and the Russian Far East. Most winter in eastern and southern China, especially around the middle and lower Yangtze River.
sections.identification: The wild bird has a striking two-tone head and neck: a dark chestnut crown and hindneck contrast with a pale face, throat, and front of the neck. Its long black bill has a narrow pale band at the base, and the legs are orange; the body is grey-brown with lighter feather edges and a pale belly. Adults are about 81–94 cm long, with a 160–185 cm wingspan and a mass of roughly 2.8–3.5 kg; body height and width are not routinely reported. Males average larger, with longer necks and heavier bills, but plumage alone does not reliably distinguish the sexes.
sections.habitat: During breeding, it uses steppe and forest-steppe wetlands: river valleys and deltas, wet meadows, and the margins of freshwater or brackish lakes. In winter, it shifts to lowland marshes, lakes, rice fields, estuaries, and tidal flats.
sections.diet: It is herbivorous, grazing on wetland plants and grasses and taking sedges, reeds, seeds, and berries as food availability changes through the year. At Shengjin Lake in China, wintering birds have been recorded eating underground Vallisneria tubers as well as sedges and canary grass.
sections.behavior: The species migrates between distant breeding and wintering areas using two broad East Asian flyways. Satellite tracking shows that individual journeys include several stopover wetlands rather than one uninterrupted flight.
sections.reproduction: Pairs arrive on breeding grounds in spring and nest in grass or reeds on a dry mound close to water, defending a small territory. Most accounts describe one clutch of about five or six eggs, incubated for roughly four weeks; family groups remain together as the goslings grow.
sections.ecology: Its closest familiar relative is the Greylag Goose, Anser anser, described in the Greylag profile. The wild Swan Goose has a longer, darker bill and a sharper pale-and-chestnut head pattern; the Greylag has a shorter pink or orange bill and a more mottled grey-brown head. Chinese domestic geese descend from the Swan Goose, whereas most European domestic geese descend from the Greylag; feral birds and hybrids can blur these field marks.
sections.conservation: BirdLife International’s 2023 global assessment lists the Swan Goose as Endangered and estimates 36,000–43,500 mature individuals, with a decreasing trend. More than 99% follow the inland flyway, concentrating risks from wetland loss, drought, hunting, egg collection, and disturbance.
